Household
HOWS-hohld
n.
House + hold; renders the Greek oikos (house, household), oikia (dwelling, family), and oikeios (of the household); and the Hebrew bayith (house, household).

📖 Biblical Definition

The household in Scripture is the primary covenantal unit—the dwelling-place and people God deals with as a body across the testaments, the first sphere of discipleship and obedience, and the basic ecclesial cell out of which the wider church is built. The Old Testament covenant is administered to households from Abraham forward: I will be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee; he that is born in thy house, and he that is bought with thy money, must needs be circumcised; the Passover is observed by households (a lamb for an house); the Shema is to be taught diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house. The New Testament continues the pattern. The Philippian jailer believes and is baptized, he and all his, straightway; Cornelius’s household receives the Spirit and is baptized; Lydia and her household are baptized; the Stephanas household are the firstfruits of Achaia. The apostle calls believers the household of faith (Gal 6:10) and the household of God (Eph 2:19; 1 Tim 3:15). Christ’s pastoral application is direct: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me—the household is real but never supreme; and every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, shall receive an hundredfold—the household and the gospel may come into conflict, and where they do, the gospel wins. The biblical doctrine of the household is therefore high. It is a covenantal unit, not merely a social arrangement. It is the first sphere of discipleship—parents to children, husband to wife, master to servant, all under the headship of Christ. It is the basic ecclesial cell—the church meets in houses across the New Testament (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19; Col 4:15; Philem 2). And it has its officers and duties: the husband as head, the wife as helper, the children as obedient, the parents as those who provoke not their children to wrath but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The household well-ordered is the foundation of the church well-ordered; the household disordered is the church disordered; and the recovery of biblical household life is, in any age, part of the recovery of biblical church life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HOUSEHOLD as those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; in scripture, the primary covenantal unit through which God deals with His people across the testaments.

expand to see more

HOUSEHOLD, n. — 1. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; those who belong to the family. Greet the household of Stephanas (1 Cor 16:15). 2. Family life; domestic management.

HOUSEHOLDER, n. — The master or chief of a family; one who occupies a house with his family. Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder (Matt 13:52).

📖 Key Scripture

Joshua 24:15 — "...as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

Acts 16:31 — "And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house."

Ephesians 2:19 — "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God."

1 Timothy 3:15 — "But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The household is corrupted, on one side, by the radical-individualism of late-modern culture that treats persons as autonomous units and dissolves the household as a covenantal category—and on the other by the household-idolatry that absolutizes family over Christ, against Christ’s own command that no household relation comes before Him.

expand to see more

Radical individualism is the most pervasive contemporary corruption. Late-modern Western culture treats persons as autonomous individuals whose primary relations are to the state and the market and whose household connections are voluntary, contingent, dissolvable, and largely sentimental. The covenantal household of Scripture—a real, structured, covenantally-administered unit with appointed offices and duties, the first sphere of discipleship, the basic ecclesial cell—has been disassembled into a loose collection of autonomous individuals who happen to share a dwelling. The recovery is the recovery of the household as a structural reality: the husband as head, the wife as helper, the children as those being discipled, the household as a body engaged together in worship, in mission, in mutual care, in the long discipleship of the next generation. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD—Joshua’s covenantal headship of his household is not a relic of patriarchal culture but the biblical pattern God’s people are to recover in every age.

The opposite corruption is the household-idolatry that absolutizes family over Christ. The household is a great good, but a created good, and like every created good it can be made into a rival of the Christ who gave it. Christ’s warning is severe: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. The household is to be loved deeply, ordered carefully, and stewarded faithfully—but not absolutized. Where it is absolutized, it produces a Christianity that will not call its children to mission costs, that will not forsake houses or lands for Christ’s sake, that treats the family as the supreme value and the gospel as instrumental to its flourishing. Recover both ends: the household as a real, structured, covenantal sphere of discipleship and obedience (against the radical-individualist corruption), and the household as a created good ordered under Christ rather than rivaling Him (against the household-idolatry)—and the biblical pattern emerges: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek oikos (house, household) and oikeios (of the household—Eph 2:19; Gal 6:10; 1 Tim 5:8); Hebrew bayith (house, household)—the primary covenantal unit through which God deals with His people, the first sphere of discipleship, and the basic ecclesial cell.

expand to see more

Greek oikos (G3624) — house, household, family, dwelling.

Greek oikia (G3614) — dwelling, household.

Greek oikeios (G3609) — of the household, member of the household (Gal 6:10; Eph 2:19; 1 Tim 5:8).

Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, household (the great OT covenantal noun).

Usage

"As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD—Joshua’s covenantal headship is the biblical pattern of household life under God."

"The household is the first sphere of discipleship and the basic ecclesial cell; the New Testament church meets in houses across the Epistles."

"Radical individualism dissolves the household as a covenantal category; household-idolatry absolutizes it over Christ; biblical doctrine holds it as a real, structured, ordered-under-Christ sphere of life."
